state_update.alternative_thought: I messed up one time because I was tired, but that doesn't mean I'm failing everything.

turns.response: That sounds like a solid start. Which specific part of that sentence feels the most true to you right now—the fact that it was just one instance, or the idea that you aren't failing everything?

turns.patient_response: The 'not failing everything' part. Because honestly, I am passing. If I said 'I'm doing great,' that would feel fake. But saying I'm not failing feels... accurate.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: not failing feels... accurate

patient_understanding.information_gap: Confirming if this nuanced statement fully replaces the original automatic thought for them.

state_update.alternative_thought: I am passing my classes even when tired, so falling asleep once does not mean I am failing everything.

turns.response: It makes sense to keep it grounded in what you know to be true rather than forcing positivity. So, if you hold onto the idea that 'falling asleep once does not mean I am failing everything,' does that help lower the feeling that you are letting your mom down?

turns.patient_response: Yeah, it takes some pressure off. I still feel guilty about sleeping, but I don't think she's mad. It's more manageable.

state_update.alternative_thought: Falling asleep once due to tiredness does not mean I am failing everything or letting family down.

turns.response: It is good that the guilt feels more manageable now. To help prevent this from happening again, what small step could you take before class to ensure you are rested enough to stay awake?

new_simulated_details: Patient considers setting a phone alarm to remind them to stop scrolling Instagram at 11:30 PM.

turns.patient_response: I don't know... maybe just trying to sleep earlier? I usually stay up because I'm looking at my phone.

turns.response: You mentioned that staying up late is often due to looking at your phone. What is one specific thing you could do with your phone tonight to help yourself put it down earlier?

turns.patient_response: Hmm. Maybe set an alarm? Like, when it goes off, I have to stop scrolling and get ready for bed. It's hard to just stop though.

turns.patient_response: I guess I'd just lock the screen and put the phone across the room. Then I can't reach it easily. That seems doable for tomorrow night.

record_update.background: Originally from the San Gabriel Valley suburb of LA; previously lived in Las Vegas and the Inland Empire before moving back to LA to care for mother-in-law. Raised primarily by her single mother and grandmother. Studied music technology and vocal performance. Sings in an opera company and works a flexible call center job catering to performers. Married for several years. Regrets sacrificing 10 years of building her own career and credit history to care for her mother.
record_update.current_medication: Takes insulin for diabetes; had to take additional medication after developing pulmonary embolisms two weeks after her mother's death.
record_update.medical_history: Diabetic (diabetes runs in the family). Neglected self-care during her mother's final year, eating poorly and mismanaging insulin, leading to high blood sugar and insulin resistance. Developed bilateral pulmonary embolisms two weeks after her mother's death due to neglecting her health. Mother-in-law currently has dementia.
record_update.mental_health_history: Experienced severe depressive episodes tied to circumstances. After her mother died four years ago, fell into deep depression, stayed in bed all day, pushed her husband away, and almost got divorced. Describes a "downer temperament" and ongoing anxiety cycles with "what if" worries about finances and stability.
record_update.previous_treatment: Has not sought professional treatment or seen a doctor for depression because she does not want to know and prefers pulling herself out of it on her own.
record_update.recent_stressor: Ongoing stress from caring for mother-in-law with dementia, including disagreement with husband about whether she should move in with them; financial anxiety about paying rent and maintaining stability.
record_update.social_support: Lives with husband and cats; moderately close to remaining family (aunt, cousins) but not in daily contact. Lost a lot of family in the last 10 years. Does not have many close friends and prefers keeping to herself.
record_update.trauma_history: Mother became ill the weekend she graduated college, requiring her to abandon a lined-up job to become her full-time caregiver for about 10 years. Mother died four years ago after a health catastrophe involving kidney failure and a stroke at age 51. Lost a lot of family members over the past 10 years.

record_update.background: The participant is originally from Los Angeles and works extensively with elders on their reservation and other reservations in California. record_update.recent_stressor: Three days ago, the participant had an argument with someone they spend almost every minute of their day with due to that person's lack of communication, leaving the participant feeling caught off guard and excluded from a situation. record_update.substance_use: During their time as a professional athlete, the participant would party until 4 in the morning before competing at 10 in the morning. They currently state they do not party.
record_update.trauma_history: The participant attributes their broken sleep and physical toll to their years as a professional fighter. They experience vivid, realistic dreams involving fighting and preparing fighters, which build anxiety and cause them to act out in their sleep. They were triggered by quick movements during their PTSD therapy.

record_update.background: The participant lives in Los Angeles. They are not currently in school but aspire to be a psychologist, having had an interest since junior high. They previously faced a decision between an admitted program and four years of art school. Before their illness onset around 1997, they were in a very good place regarding career, relationships, and personal fulfillment. They describe themselves as shy but outgoing, compassionate, and empathetic despite coming from an abusive environment. They regret trusting medical professionals blindly prior to their ER injury.
record_update.medical_history: The participant went to the emergency room for food poisoning after collapsing and was injured during an intravenous procedure, developing reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD) / complex regional pain syndrome. This resulted in permanent disability, limited functionality in their right hand and arm (they are right-handed), disfigurement, and ongoing excruciating physical pain, severe fatigue, and feeling very ill. They note being in a good career place before this illness began around July 1997.
record_update.mental_health_history: The participant reports diagnoses received 3 years ago and in 2001 (around age 20). They identify having PTSD, agoraphobia (a more recent, progressing development), fear of flying, depression, anxiety, severe nightmares, nocturnal panic attacks, and disturbing thoughts triggered by their injury, family treatment, and physical illness.
record_update.previous_treatment: The participant was in therapy but stopped 6 months ago, describing it as a break with plans to continue. They report therapy helped tremendously with anxiety, inspiration, feeling connected, giving themselves a voice, and understanding themselves. They also use bibliotherapy, reading professional literature to cope with agoraphobia.
record_update.recent_stressor: The participant's cat was recently in intensive veterinary care. The participant also reports ongoing excruciating physical pain, severe fatigue, and worsening agoraphobia as current stressors.
record_update.social_support: The participant has no relationship with their family since being estranged at age 21; they describe the majority of their family as very cruel and abusive, though an aunt, uncle, and cousins were previously the loving aspect before a temporary falling out. The participant continuously interacts with people, including someone named Rachel, and values meaningful human connection.
record_update.trauma_history: The participant reports childhood abuse from their family of origin, followed by rejection and estrangement at age 21 when their aunt and uncle disowned them after a disagreement. They also experienced medical trauma when an intravenous procedure in the emergency room went wrong, resulting in permanent disability, disfigurement, and residual physical trauma.

new_simulated_details: The patient recently had a scheduled appointment to pick up their cat from the veterinary clinic.
They declined the ride because they felt unable to get into the car due to worsening agoraphobia.
They experienced intense physical pain and panic symptoms while sitting in their living room waiting for the appointment time.

turns.patient_response: I guess I just want to talk about how hard it is to leave the house. It's been getting worse lately, like immobilizing me completely.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: how hard it is to leave the house
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Frustration and distress regarding progressive agoraphobia.
patient_understanding.information_gap: A specific recent event illustrating this difficulty has not yet been identified.

question_plan.question_target: Identify one concrete recent episode where the agoraphobia significantly impacted the patient.

turns.response: It sounds like that feeling of being immobilized is really weighing on you right now. To help us understand that better, can you think of one specific moment recently—perhaps related to your cat or another errand—where you noticed that reaction strongly?

turns.patient_response: Well, last week I was supposed to go pick my cat up from the vet after her intensive care stay. But when the time came, I just couldn't get into the car. I sat here in the living room for an hour, feeling sick and terrified.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: couldn't get into the car
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Relief at identifying a concrete example mixed with residual shame/fear.
patient_understanding.information_gap: None; the situation is sufficiently detailed for CBT exploration.

question_plan.question_target: Identify the automatic thought or mental image present during the agoraphobic episode.

state_update.situation: Last week, the patient was unable to enter their car to pick up their cat from the veterinary clinic due to severe agoraphobic anxiety, remaining in the living room for an hour.

turns.response: Thank you for sharing that specific moment; sitting in the living room while feeling terrified is a powerful example of how immobilizing this can be. When you were stuck there, unable to get into the car to pick up your cat, what was going through your mind?

new_simulated_details: The patient initially struggles to identify a single thought, offering general anxiety instead.
The patient recalls a specific mental image of the car door locking and trapping them inside.
The patient identifies the core automatic thought as 'I will be trapped and unable to get back home.'

turns.patient_response: I'm not sure if I had one specific sentence in my head. It was more like... just this wave of dread? Does that count as a thought?

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: just this wave of dread
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Uncertainty about distinguishing emotion from cognition; feeling overwhelmed by physical sensations of anxiety.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Need to help the patient separate the feeling of dread from the cognitive prediction or image associated with it.

question_plan.question_target: Ask the patient to describe what the 'dread' felt like it was warning them about, to uncover the underlying prediction.

turns.response: That's a very common experience when anxiety is high—the line between feeling and thinking can blur. If you imagine that 'wave of dread' could speak, what would it say is happening if you try to open that car door?

turns.patient_response: Hmm, okay. If it spoke... I think it would say something like 'You're going to get stuck.' Or maybe 'You won't make it back.' Is that what you mean?

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: You won't make it back
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Emerging recognition of catastrophic predictions; tentative identification of a core fear.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Confirming which of these predictions feels most central to the paralysis experienced in the living room.

question_plan.question_target: Ask the patient to identify which of the proposed thoughts ('getting stuck' vs 'not making it back') felt most urgent or immobilizing at that moment.

state_update.automatic_thought: Predictions of getting stuck or not making it back

turns.response: Yes, exactly those kinds of predictions. Between 'you're going to get stuck' and 'you won't make it back,' which one felt louder or more important to your decision to stay in the living room?

turns.patient_response: 'I won't make it back.' That was the big one. Like, if I leave, I'm never coming home again. That's why I couldn't move. So... how does that connect to how I felt?

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: I won't make it back
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Clarity on the primary automatic thought; curiosity about its link to emotional state.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Transitioning from identifying the thought to exploring the specific emotions triggered by this belief.

question_plan.question_target: Identify the primary emotion linked to the automatic thought during the agoraphobic episode.

state_update.automatic_thought: If I leave, I'm never coming home again.

turns.response: That thought—'If I leave, I'm never coming home again'—seems to be the core reason you felt unable to move. When that specific fear was running through your mind while you sat in the living room, what was the strongest emotion you felt?

new_simulated_details: The patient describes the emotion as a mix of terror and helplessness.
The patient rates the intensity of the terror as an 8 out of 10.

turns.patient_response: It was mostly terror. Just pure panic that I'd be trapped somewhere else, not here where it's safe. It felt like my chest was tight.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: mostly terror
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Experiencing intense fear and physical anxiety symptoms.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Need to distinguish between the bodily sensation (tightness) and the emotional label, and check for other co-existing emotions.

question_plan.question_target: Clarify if the tightness is just a physical symptom or if there is an accompanying feeling like sadness or anger.

state_update.emotion: Terror and panic accompanied by physical tightness.

turns.response: I hear you. That tightness in your chest sounds like a very real physical reaction to that fear. Besides the terror itself, did you notice any other feelings mixed in, perhaps something like frustration or sadness about being unable to go?

turns.patient_response: Yeah... definitely frustration. Like, why can't I just do this? Everyone else gets in their car and goes. But underneath that, it was this deep helplessness. I felt small.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: deep helplessness
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Feeling frustrated with self but primarily experiencing profound helplessness and vulnerability.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Need to prioritize which emotion was most dominant at the peak of the situation to focus the CBT work.

question_plan.question_target: Determine which of the identified emotions (terror, frustration, helplessness) was the strongest driver during the hour in the living room.

turns.response: Thank you for naming those; 'helplessness' is a powerful word that captures that feeling of being small against the fear. Out of terror, frustration, and helplessness, which one felt the most intense or overwhelming while you were sitting there?

turns.patient_response: The helplessness. The terror was scary, but the helplessness made me give up. If I had to rate it, maybe an 8? Because it just froze me completely.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: The helplessness
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Identifies helplessness as the primary blocking emotion, rated 8/10 intensity.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Emotion stage is complete; need to transition to behavior to see what actions followed this specific feeling.

question_plan.question_target: Identify specific actions, inactions, or unacted urges during the agoraphobic episode.

turns.response: An 8/10 for helplessness that completely froze you is a heavy burden to carry, and it makes sense that such intense paralysis would dictate your actions in that moment. In response to that feeling of being frozen while sitting in the living room, what did you actually do, or was there an urge you felt but didn't act on?

new_simulated_details: The patient remained in the living room for an hour.
The patient eventually called a friend to pick up the cat instead of going themselves.

turns.patient_response: I just sat there. I couldn't move my legs. It felt like they were made of lead. I stared at the door but didn't get up.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: I just sat there
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Helplessness (8/10) causing physical paralysis/inaction.
patient_understanding.information_gap: What happened after the initial freezing? Did the situation resolve, or did they remain stuck?

question_plan.question_target: Identify subsequent actions or avoidance behaviors following the initial freeze response.

state_update.behavior: Sat frozen in the living room, unable to move towards the car.

turns.response: It sounds like that helplessness truly immobilized you in that moment. After sitting there frozen for a while, what was the next thing you did, or how long did you stay in that state?

turns.patient_response: I stayed there for about an hour. The anxiety didn't go down enough to make me drive. So... I think I finally picked up the phone and called Rachel to ask her to get the cat for me.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: called Rachel to ask her to get the cat
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Relief mixed with shame; acknowledgment of avoidance via delegation.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Understanding the purpose of this specific action (calling Rachel) in relation to the fear.

question_plan.question_target: Explore the immediate intent or perceived benefit of calling Rachel instead of facing the agoraphobic trigger.

state_update.behavior: Remained in living room for one hour, then avoided driving by calling Rachel to pick up the cat.

turns.response: Thank you for sharing that detail; it helps clarify how you managed the situation when your own resources felt depleted. When you decided to call Rachel to handle the pickup, what were you hoping that action would do for you in that moment?

turns.patient_response: I guess I hoped it would stop the panic. If I didn't have to leave, I wouldn't be trapped out there. It felt like the only way to feel safe again without forcing myself into the danger zone.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: hoped it would stop the panic
patient_understanding.current_belief_or_emotion: Safety-seeking behavior driven by the belief that leaving equals permanent entrapment.
patient_understanding.information_gap: Transitioning from behavior description to examining the evidence supporting the automatic thought.

question_plan.question_target: Identify specific evidence supporting the automatic thought

turns.patient_response: Well... it’s mostly because I’ve been stuck before. Like, once when I went to the grocery store, I had such bad anxiety that I couldn’t drive back for hours. I had to call my friend to come get me. It just feels like if I leave, I lose control of getting back.

patient_understanding.patient_anchor: I had to call my friend to come get me

turns.response: That sounds like a genuinely frightening experience that would naturally make you wary of driving alone again. Are there other recent times or situations where you felt similarly unable to return on your own terms?

turns.patient_response: Yes, exactly. And lately, with this RSD pain in my right hand, it’s hard to even hold the keys sometimes. If I’m in so much pain at home, how can I trust I’d be okay out there? The pain makes me feel disabled and trapped inside, so going out feels dangerous.

record_update.background: He has lived in his current location since 1946. He worked as a merchant seaman traveling to different countries, including Japan, and learned multiple languages. He has diverse skills including electronics, broadcast technology, brick masonry, tailoring, fashion design, hair styling, and sign language interpreting. He is a veteran who spent about 20 to 30 years homeless after returning from the war before moving into a veteran sanctuary. He is married.
record_update.current_medication: He takes Seroquel for sleep but has recently been trying to reduce its use, reporting some success falling asleep without it despite sleeping fewer hours and waking up often.
record_update.medical_history: unknown
record_update.mental_health_history: He reports a 50% service-connected disability rating related to PTSD and depression. He describes long-standing symptoms including no sleep, nightmares, waking up fighting, and intrusive thoughts. He attributes much of his distress to internal processes rather than external events.
record_update.previous_treatment: He has not been in therapy in the past year but wants to return because he feels he needs it. He values therapy that provides live feedback from men with similar overall experiences. He also researches his own psychological profile through books, studies, philosophy, metaphysics, prayer, and meditation for self-preservation and family safety.
record_update.recent_stressor: The participant reports intrusive thoughts occurring every day for the past two or three months, which he finds frightening. He also recently had a conflict with another veteran who was disciplining children at his residence.
record_update.social_support: He currently lives in a veteran sanctuary where he feels somewhat welcome and appreciates his case manager, property manager, and others involved in his healing. He considers his mother his best friend. He reports having learned to stay detached from feelings and people during the war, making it difficult to form friendships, though he is now learning how to be a friend.
record_update.trauma_history: He served as a merchant seaman and then in the military, spending a couple of years in a war zone (Vietnam) around 1967. He experienced moral injury after requesting conscientious objector status, which caused problems in the war zone, and describes a suicidal attempt to kill someone else. He reports killing someone who did not deserve to die. Upon returning home, he felt unwelcome and labeled a "baby killer" for 20 to 30 years while living on the ground. He also describes unknowingly kicking his wife out of bed at night and giving her a black eye, possibly due to feeling like he was still in Vietnam.

record_update.background: Originally from North Carolina, he moved to Los Angeles almost four years ago after college for a production company internship and stayed for the resources and accessibility to pursue his passions. He studied history, media studies, and production, and has worked as a freelance writer and producer for a little over a year. He travels internationally every six to seven months. He finds it difficult when people are upset with him and hates letting people down.
record_update.medical_history: Sleep difficulties include sometimes waking within an hour of falling asleep and being unable to return to sleep, or waking periodically. Sleep improved somewhat in recent weeks but worsens when his girlfriend is away. Exercise has been a huge help for sleep.
record_update.mental_health_history: Diagnosed with depression once in high school, and experienced a second depressive episode within the past year characterized by severe insomnia (one hour or no sleep), loss of drive for basic hygiene and cleaning, and general malaise. He views depression as something he must keep in check throughout his life, noting that creative people are prone to self-esteem issues.
record_update.previous_treatment: He saw a therapist within the past year after recognizing returning depressive symptoms and realizing he could not fight it alone. He discontinued therapy after graduating from it, feeling he had talked through what he needed to, that his life was in a good place with meaningful work and a relationship, and that he no longer had time due to work demands.
record_update.recent_stressor: Freelance work gaps cause anxiety about what comes next; the participant feels depressed and jealous of those with stable office jobs because all responsibility falls on him. His girlfriend travels frequently for work, leaving them separated by distance for weeks at a time, which is sad and disrupts his sleep.
record_update.social_support: He has a girlfriend who is a major source of comfort and happiness when present, though they are often separated by her travel. He maintains close friendships, many on the East Coast, whom he calls regularly, and describes himself as selfless and reliable for friends. He values therapy as having someone to confide in outside of friends or family.
record_update.trauma_history: His younger sister died when he was about 12 years old. Watching his father cry for the first time and seeing his parents deal with losing a child was very traumatic, making him feel he grew up significantly that day and shaping how he copes with hardships.

record_update.background: He is a 68-year-old retired Jewish chaplain originally from Boston, Massachusetts, with a Psychology degree from Boston College. He joined the military at age 17 and served 4 years and 2 months in the Air Force during the Vietnam War, stationed in Europe. After the military he started and ran a business while continuing as a volunteer chaplain for 52 years. He currently volunteers at a women's prison in Chino and conducts services at a Jewish community he established over 51 years ago. He is divorced after a 16-year marriage that resulted in a 13-year acrimonious divorce; his parents are deceased.
record_update.medical_history: He became quite ill a few years ago and underwent open heart surgery, taking about two years to become healthy again. Since the surgery he has been relatively healthy. He sleeps easily for 6 to 7 hours and bounces back quickly from minor illnesses like colds or flu.
record_update.mental_health_history: He explicitly states he has never been diagnosed with PTSD.
record_update.previous_treatment: He has not been going to therapy himself but believes it is useful, noting that many veterans he lives and works with have had extensive therapy that proved very successful.
record_update.recent_stressor: An argument several months ago with someone he was dating about her inappropriate language. His former wife created legal problems for him during their acrimonious divorce, which took 13 years to resolve.
record_update.social_support: He is quite outgoing and comfortable meeting strangers. He has a 27-year-old daughter who is the light of his life, and a brother and sister-in-law living in Boston. He is very involved in the veteran community, works with clergy mentors, and attends social events like birthday parties.
record_update.trauma_history: He served in the Air Force during the Vietnam War as a chaplain stationed in Europe. He reports he never saw combat, was never shot at, and never had to kill anyone. About 55 of the 60 people he trained with went to Vietnam and fewer than 50 returned, representing high mortality among peers.
